title: Siege of Sarajevo
wiki_lead:
The Siege of Sarajevo (Serbian: Опсада Сарајева; Croatian: Opsada Sarajeva) was a prolonged military blockade of Sarajevo, the capital of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, during the Bosnian War. Beginning on 5 April 1992, the capital was surrounded by Bosnian Serb forces following the outbreak of the Bosnian War. After the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) from Bosnia and Herzegovina, much of its Bosnian Serb personnel, weaponry and equipment were transferred to the newly established Army of Republika Srpska (VRS), which continued the blockade. The siege lasted until 29 February 1996, spanning 1,425 days. It was nearly twice as long as the siege of Leningrad and is widely regarded as the longest siege of a capital city in the history of modern warfare.
Following the declaration of independence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia after the 1992 independence referendum, Bosnian Serb forces encircled Sarajevo with an initial force of approximately 13,000 soldiers, establishing strategic positions in the surrounding hills. The political objective of the Bosnian Serb leadership was to establish a Bosnian Serb state, Republika Srpska (RS), encompassing territories inhabited by Bosniaks and other non-Serb populations. The besieging forces imposed a military blockade on the city and subjected it to sustained bombardment using artillery, tanks, mortars, and small arms, including sniper fire. An estimated 500,000 shells were fired at Sarajevo over the course of the siege.
The Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina (ARBiH), alongside elements of the Croatian Defence Council (HVO), maintained a force of approximately 70,000 troops within Sarajevo. Despite its considerable manpower, the ARBiH was significantly outmatched in heavy weaponry. At the beginning of the siege, Bosnian Serb forces controlled several suburbs surrounding the city, including Ilidža, Nedžarići, and parts of Grbavica. Meanwhile, other areas of Sarajevo experienced intense urban combat, characterized by street-to-street fighting. Clashes were particularly fierce during the opening months of the siege, although direct engagements became less frequent as the conflict progressed. The ARBiH retained control over much of central and eastern Sarajevo, although several neighbourhoods along the city's outskirts remained vulnerable to Bosnian Serb positions. Repeated attempts by the ARBiH to break through the encirclement proved unsuccessful, resulting in substantial casualties among its defenders.
The intensity of the attacks made Sarajevo one of the most dangerous cities for civilians, including children, who faced the daily risk of death or injury from indiscriminate shelling and sniper fire while moving through the city. United Nations (UN) personnel stationed in the city also faced considerable danger during peacekeeping and humanitarian operations, suffering fatalities and injuries from artillery fire, sniper attacks, land mine explosions, and assaults on UN positions. Humanitarian aid aircraft participating in Operation Provide Promise were also frequently targeted by ground fire. On 3 September 1992, an Italian Aeritalia G.222 transport aircraft was shot down by a shoulder-fired surface-to-air missile while approaching Sarajevo. The aircraft crashed approximately 35 kilometres west of the city, killing all four crew members.
A total of 13,952 people were killed during the siege, including 5,434 civilians. Among the military casualties, the ARBiH suffered 6,137 fatalities, while the VRS lost 2,241 soldiers. According to the 1991 census, Sarajevo and its surrounding areas had a combined population of 525,980. Estimates of the population within the city proper before the siege ranged from 435,000. Following the siege, Sarajevo's population was estimated to have fallen to between 300,000 to 380,000. During certain periods of the siege, residents endured prolonged shortages of essential utilities, with some areas experiencing interruptions to gas, electricity, and water supplies lasting up to six months. 
Following the second Markale massacre on 28 August 1995, NATO initiated Operation Deliberate Force, a sustained air campaign targeting Bosnian Serb military positions across Bosnia and Herzegovina, including those in the vicinity of Sarajevo. The campaign, combined with mounting international pressure, contributed to the eventual cessation of hostilities. A ceasefire took effect in October 1995, followed by the signing of the Dayton Peace Agreement on 14 December 1995. The siege was officially declared over on 29 February 1996, although the transfer of Serb-controlled Sarajevo suburbs and the city's reunification continued into March 1996.
After the war, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) found that Bosnian Serb forces carried out a sustained campaign of sniping and shelling that deliberately targeted civilians, as well as indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks across the city, resulting in thousands of civilian death and injuries. Four Bosnian Serb officials were convicted for numerous counts of crimes against humanity committed during the siege, including terrorism. Stanislav Galić and Dragomir Milošević were sentenced to life imprisonment and 29 years imprisonment respectively. Their superiors, Radovan Karadžić  and Ratko Mladić, were also convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment.

grok_lead: The Siege of Sarajevo was a military encirclement and bombardment of Bosnia and Herzegovina's capital city, initially by Serbian forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and subsequently by Bosnian Serb forces of the Army of Republika Srpska (VRS), beginning on 5 April 1992 amid the breakup of Yugoslavia and the ensuing Bosnian War. The VRS, seeking to establish control over territories claimed for the self-proclaimed Republika Srpska, positioned artillery and snipers on surrounding hills to isolate and attack the city held by the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina (ARBiH). Lasting 1,425 days until early 1996, it was three times longer than the Battle of Stalingrad and stands as the longest siege of a capital in modern warfare, surpassing previous records like the 872-day Siege of Leningrad in World War II. The siege involved relentless shelling and sniper fire targeting civilian areas, markets, and infrastructure, restricting food, water, and medical supplies to over 300,000 residents through blockades and attacks on humanitarian convoys. Empirical estimates place the death toll from siege-related violence at approximately 9,500 in the core Sarajevo municipalities, predominantly civilians, though figures vary due to challenges in attributing casualties amid mutual combat and disputed records from conflicting parties. International efforts, including UN peacekeeping under UNPROFOR and eventual NATO airstrikes, failed to fully lift the blockade until the 1995 Dayton Agreement, which partitioned Bosnia and compelled VRS withdrawal. Key controversies surround the siege's conduct, with VRS leaders like Ratko MladiÄ and Radovan KaradÅ¾iÄ later convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia of crimes against humanity for deliberately terrorizing civilians, yet some analyses question the completeness of investigations into ARBiH self-shelling or propaganda-exaggerated incidents to elicit Western intervention. The event exemplified the ethnic fracturing of multi-ethnic Sarajevo, where pre-war Bosniak, Serb, and Croat communities coexisted, but post-independence violence drove demographic shifts and enduring divisions. Despite underground tunnels enabling limited supplies and resistance, the siege inflicted profound humanitarian crisis, with survivors enduring starvation, disease, and psychological trauma.
